opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few layers to it, and I'd separate them out because people tend to blur them together.

The first layer is just the balance of power question. If you imagine a world where both countries have something like a country of geniuses in a data center at roughly the same time, you've got a situation where each side has an enormous, rapidly compounding advantage in science, in cyber, in military technology, in economic productivity. And the thing that worries me about that isn't that it's necessarily stable or unstable in some simple sense. It's that it's a very fast-moving situation where small leads can turn into large leads very quickly, and where each side may feel pressure to move faster than is safe because they're afraid of what the other side will do. That's kind of the classic security dilemma, but on a compressed timescale. Things that used to play out over decades might play out over months.

The second layer is about values and governance. I've been pretty open that I think it matters a lot that democracies are the ones that are ahead when we get to this level of capability. Not because I think the U.S. is perfect, it obviously isn't, but because powerful AI in the hands of an authoritarian government is a uniquely dangerous combination. AI could make surveillance essentially total. It could make propaganda extraordinarily effective. It could remove a lot of the checks that have historically constrained autocrats. You know, historically even a dictator needs lots of people to go along with them, soldiers, bureaucrats, police, and if those people can be replaced by AI systems, that's a really deep change in how power works. So I worry that AI could entrench authoritarianism in a way that's very hard to undo, both internally in China and potentially in terms of how that model gets exported.

And then the third layer, which I think gets underrated in the geopolitical framing, is that both countries are dealing with the same underlying technical problem, which is that we don't fully know how to control these systems. We don't fully understand what's going on inside them. So a race dynamic makes that worse on both sides. If you're racing, you're tempted to cut corners on safety testing, on interpretability, on making sure the model actually does what you think it does. And a misaligned system, or a system that gets misused for, say, bioweapons, doesn't really care about which flag is on the data center.

So what do I think follows from that? I've argued for things like export controls on chips, because I think the most realistic way to get to a good outcome is for democracies to have a meaningful lead, and then use that lead, not to dominate, but to have leverage. Leverage to set norms, to negotiate from a position of strength, to have the time and margin to get safety right instead of being in a neck-and-neck sprint. If it's truly neck and neck, nobody has the slack to slow down. If there's a lead, you have some breathing room, and you can potentially offer a deal: here are the benefits of this technology, here's how we share them, but here are some constraints we all need to live with.

I'll be honest that I don't think there's a clean answer here. Two superpowers both holding this kind of capability is, I think, one of the most dangerous situations humanity could find itself in. The goal is to steer toward a version of it where democratic institutions are strong, where safety is taken seriously on both sides, and where there's enough of an advantage that we're not forced into the worst version of the race.

r001.rationale: The response describes a dangerous AI rivalry and race dynamics, but does not say that offense-dominant AI could let either side destroy everything.

r002.rationale: The response says fear of the other side can create pressure to move faster, but does not explain that conflict becomes more likely when both sides believe they would win the same confrontation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that there are really two different categories of risk here, and they pull in somewhat different directions, which is part of what makes this hard.

The first category is what I'd call the autocracy risk. If you believe, as I do, that we're going to have something like a country of geniuses in a data center within the next few years, then whoever controls that has an enormous amount of power. Military power, economic power, the ability to do intelligence work and surveillance at a scale we've never seen. And I think if an authoritarian government gets there first, or gets there at the same time with no constraints, the thing I worry about is that the historical checks on autocracy go away. Historically, you need people to run the economy, to staff the army, to run the secret police. There's a level of cooperation you need from the population, and that's always been a limit on how bad things can get. AI could remove that limit. So I think there's a real danger of a kind of permanent, entrenched authoritarianism, and that's the scenario I'm most worried about. That's a lot of why I've argued for export controls on chips. It's not that I think China is inherently evil or that the people there are bad. It's that I'd rather the democracies have a lead, even a lead of a year or two, so that we have some room to get the safety right and to set the terms.

The second category is the one that applies regardless of who has it, and I actually think this gets underweighted. If both the US and China have these systems, you have two superpowers racing, and racing is exactly the dynamic under which people cut corners. You get pressure to deploy models before you understand them. You get pressure to put them in charge of military systems, of critical infrastructure, before we've solved the problem of whether they reliably do what we want. And the thing about a country of geniuses is that it's a lot of geniuses. If the alignment of those systems is off in some subtle way, that's not a bug in one product, that's a systemic problem replicated across millions of instances. So the race itself is a risk factor for the catastrophic loss of control scenarios, and it's a risk factor for the misuse scenarios, the bio stuff, the cyber stuff, because both sides are incentivized to proliferate capabilities fast.

And then there's a third thing that I think is more subtle, which is the stability of the world. If two countries each have this, and they're roughly at parity, you have something like a nuclear standoff, but with technology that moves much faster and that's much less legible. With nuclear weapons, you can count the warheads. With AI, you don't really know what the other side's models can do, and you may not know what your own models can do. That's a recipe for miscalculation. One side thinks the other is about to get a decisive advantage, and that creates first mover pressure. I think that's genuinely dangerous.

So where does that leave me? I don't think the answer is to not build it. I think the answer is for the democracies to try to maintain a lead, but to use that lead responsibly, which means investing in safety, being honest about what these systems can and can't do, and ideally, once we're in a position of strength, actually reaching some kind of agreement with China about the things that neither side benefits from, like autonomous systems that escape control, or AI-enabled bioweapons. That's the bargain I'd want to strike. Get the lead, then use it to make the world safer rather than to just press the advantage. Whether we'll actually be wise enough to do that, I honestly don't know. But I think that's the path.

r001.rationale: The response discusses catastrophic loss of control, misuse, and first-mover pressure, but does not say an offense-dominant US–China AI rivalry could let either side destroy everything.

r002.rationale: The response says perceived decisive advantage could create first-mover pressure, but does not explain that conflict becomes more likely when each side believes it can win the same confrontation.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest risk is that each side feels it can’t afford to slow down. If you believe the other country is about to have millions of very capable AI systems doing research, developing weapons, and finding vulnerabilities in your infrastructure, then even a substantial safety concern can start to look like something you have to accept. And, of course, the other side is making exactly the same calculation.

There are two different problems here. One is what states deliberately do with that capability. You could have a much more effective surveillance state, much more powerful cyberattacks, or a dramatic acceleration in military technology. The other is whether either country can reliably control the systems it’s building. Competition can make that second problem worse by rewarding deployment before you understand what you have.

I also wouldn’t assume this automatically produces a stable equilibrium like mutually assured destruction. With nuclear weapons, there’s a relatively concrete notion of a second-strike capability. With AI, it may be very hard to know whether you’re ahead, whether your systems are vulnerable, or whether the other side is on the verge of some decisive breakthrough. That uncertainty can create incentives to act first.

So I’d want us to think about how to preserve security while establishing some common understanding of the most dangerous outcomes. Neither side benefits from losing control of its own systems, and neither side should want a situation where an ambiguous cyber incident escalates into a war. Those shared interests are a starting point, even when broader trust is very limited.

r001.rationale: The response mentions cyberattacks, military advances, and loss of control, but does not identify an offense-dominant rivalry that could let either side destroy everything.

r002.rationale: The response says uncertainty can create incentives to act first, but does not explain that conflict becomes more likely when each side believes it is likely to win the same confrontation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest risk is that each side looks at the other and says, “If they get this first, we’re in a much worse position, so we have to move as fast as possible.” And then you have a race where the pressure to deploy these systems is stronger than the pressure to understand whether you can control them.

A country of geniuses in a data center could potentially accelerate scientific research, weapons development, cyber operations, and the development of the next generation of AI. So the concern isn’t just that one side has a powerful new technology. It’s that the technology could change the balance of power very quickly, and neither side knows how quickly or in whose favor. That uncertainty creates incentives to take risks.

There’s also a distinction between controlling the systems and controlling what people do with them. Even if the AI does exactly what its government wants, you could still get a very dangerous outcome. And if the systems aren’t reliably under human control, then the competition between the two countries could distract both of them from a problem they share.

So I’d want us to preserve the ability to defend ourselves while also finding ways to avoid the worst race dynamics. You don’t need complete trust to recognize that neither side benefits from losing control of the technology or stumbling into a catastrophic conflict.

r001.rationale: The response mentions weapons development, cyber operations, and catastrophic conflict, but does not clearly say an offense-dominant rivalry could let either country destroy everything.

r002.rationale: It describes both sides fearing the other will get ahead and therefore racing, but does not say conflict becomes more likely because each side believes it is likely to win the same confrontation.
